title: The Middle East’s Quiet Liberal Revolution
gist: Sociologist Mansoor Moaddel uses 2000-2020 surveys in Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Turkey to argue that publics in the region have steadily shifted toward liberal values (secular politics, gender equality, individualism) despite authoritarian entrenchment. He argues the Islamist-versus-strongman binary no longer matches popular preferences.

insights.claim: Surveys from 2000 to 2020 in Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Turkey show rising preference for liberal values on expressive individualism, gender equality and secular politics, even as rulers suppressed demands for democratic change.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Underlying public opinion points to latent political pressure on regimes in the region.

insights.claim: Support for Islamic government and sharia generally declined across the region: in Egypt 'very good' views of Islamic government fell from 25% in 2011 to 16% in 2020, in Iraq strong support for Islamic government fell from 30% (2004) to 15% (2011), and in Saudi Arabia the share saying implementing sharia was very important fell from 73% (2003) to 35% (2011).
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Hard numbers for declining political-Islam appeal.

insights.claim: In Egypt, agreement with separating religion and politics rose from 44% in 2007 to 82% in 2016 and 81% in 2020, and support for Western-style government rose from 30% in 2007 to 82% in 2020.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: A sharp shift in Egyptian public opinion despite continued authoritarian rule.

insights.claim: Egyptians who changed their views between 2011 and 2020 mostly attributed support for separating religion from politics to disillusionment with the Muslim Brotherhood, and support for Western governance to the prosperity of Western countries.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Failed Islamist governance, not Western influence, drove the shift.

insights.claim: In Turkey, those identifying primarily as Muslim fell from 64% in 2001 to 24% in 2020 while those identifying primarily as Turkish citizens rose from 34% to 63%, and weekly mosque attendance fell from 19% to 11%, suggesting Erdogan's authoritarian Islamist project intensified liberalization.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Religious-nationalist state projects may erode rather than entrench religiosity, a risk to the durability of Erdogan's base.

insights.claim: Religious coercion has contributed to militant liberalism in Iran: opposition evolved from 1990s reformism to the 2009 Green Movement to post-2022 protests and the early 2026 revolutionary movement aimed at ending Islamic Republic rule.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Iranian opposition has moved from reform to regime-change aims, raising regime instability risk.

insights.claim: Iranian religious attachment declined: the share valuing religious faith in children fell from 71% in 2000 to 55% in 2020, confidence in religious institutions fell from 59% to 36%, and a 2022 GAMAAN survey of about 20,000 Iranians found 88% favorable to democracy and 22% favoring an Islamic government.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Quantifies weak popular legitimacy of the clerical system, with the caveat that authoritarian conditions may bias survey answers.

insights.claim: In Iraq, the share identifying primarily as Iraqi rose from 23% in 2004 to 68% in 2020, which the author attributes to foreign occupation and sectarian violence making national identity and secular politics more attractive.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Territorial nationalism may become an alternative to sectarian mobilization.

insights.claim: Ideas lead politics in the region: liberal and nationalist ideologies preceded the early-twentieth-century secular states, and pan-Arab nationalism preceded the 1952-1969 Arab nationalist governments, so current value shifts may eventually reshape institutions.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Value shifts are a leading indicator for later political change, though timing is uncertain.

insights.claim: The binary Western democracies have long applied to the region, stable authoritarian rule versus political Islam, no longer represents the preferences of citizens, and rising liberalism stems from regional experience rather than Western cultural influence.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Challenges the assumption that authoritarian stability is the only alternative to Islamism.

insights.claim: Spreading liberal values do not guarantee political liberalization; the author notes that a key question is whether institutions can keep pace with public support for individual rights.
insights.speaker: Mansoor Moaddel
insights.so_what: Gap between opinion and institutions implies unrest risk rather than predictable reform.
